name: Cold spoons
lead: Cold spoons is a home practice in which a spoon chilled in a freezer or fridge is pressed against the skin around the eyes to reduce puffiness or bloat, so the eye area looks fresher and less swollen. People use it as a quick morning step, much like a cold compress, before going out or filming.

It borrows its logic from cold compresses. Reference material on periorbital puffiness describes a cold compress as a short-term remedy because cold narrows blood vessels, which reduces fluid leaking into the tissue and eases puffiness.[3] Puffiness around the eyes is often worst on waking because fluid shifts when a person lies flat, and other listed contributors include allergies, salt intake, lack of sleep, crying and ageing.[3]

On looksmax.org the technique is discussed in a small number of threads: one asks whether chilled spoons are legitimate for decreasing bloat, with a reply saying cold encourages blood flow and reduces swelling, and another participant recalling forum claims that ice can damage nerves.[1] No published research has tested spoons specifically.

angle.text: A chilled spoon is a cheap, quick way to apply cold to the eye area for a temporary reduction in morning puffiness. People use it to make the eyes look more rested.

paras: The practice is a variation of the cold compress: a cold object is held briefly against the skin around the eyes. Cold is described as narrowing blood vessels and reducing fluid leaking into tissue, presented as a short-term effect.[3]

Periorbital puffiness has many causes, including thin skin and an enlarging fat pad under the lower eyelids with age, allergic reactions, salt and fluid retention, sleep deprivation, alcohol and fatigue, and medical conditions such as hypothyroidism. The reference notes that severe or persistent swelling may signal an underlying condition.[3] Other approaches listed for puffiness include sleeping with the head elevated, diet and lifestyle changes, and surgery.[3]

Reference material on cold therapy reports that ice applied directly to skin can cause cold burns and that serious injuries have followed excessive cooling time with powered devices.[2] The reference does not mention nerve injury for brief use, so the nerve-damage idea raised in forum discussion is not covered by that source.[1][2]

No studies found on cold spoons. Research on cold compression in sprains and post-surgical swelling is a different setting, and a review cited by the Wikipedia article found insufficient evidence for acute ankle sprains.[2]

lore.intro: Cold spoons appear in a small number of looksmax.org threads about debloating and puffiness.[1]

claims.claim: A freezer-cold spoon reduces bloat and under-eye puffiness
claims.believers: A forum reply says cold encourages blood flow and reduces swelling.[1]
claims.experts: Reference sources describe cold compresses as a short-term remedy for puffiness because cold narrows vessels; cold compression for injury swelling has mixed evidence, and no study has tested spoons.[2][3]

claims.claim: Cold applied to the face can cause nerve damage
claims.believers: Some forum users say they read that ice packs cause nerve damage and avoid them.[1]
claims.experts: Reference material documents cold burns and tissue injury from prolonged cooling but does not mention nerve injury from brief use.[2]

card.summary: A chilled spoon on the eyes for puff; no research, mostly a forum curiosity.
card.note: Cold directly on skin can cause burns.

quick.overview:
Cold spoons are spoons chilled in the freezer and held against the eye area to reduce puffiness.

Only a thin forum discussion exists and no studies have tested it.
quick.mechanism: Cold is said to narrow blood vessels and reduce fluid in the tissue temporarily.
quick.risks: Ice directly on skin can cause cold burns; forum users also voice unverified nerve-damage worries.
